lessons.title: Claim and reason
lessons.tip: A claim is what you want people to accept: “Schools should start later.” A reason answers “why?”: “because teenagers need more sleep.” A good argument joins them with “because.” A claim without a reason is only an opinion.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Choose strong evidence
lessons.tip: Evidence is a fact, an example, a number or an expert’s view that supports a reason. Strong evidence is specific, true and connected to the claim. Weak evidence is vague (“everyone knows”), only personal (“my cousin did this”) or about something else.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Order an argument
lessons.tip: A clear argument has four parts: claim, reason, evidence and conclusion. Start with the claim, say why, prove it, and finish by repeating the claim in a stronger way. Signpost each step with words like “first,” “for example” and “therefore.”
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Phrases for arguing
lessons.tip: Good speakers use set phrases. To give an opinion: “In my opinion…,” “I believe…” To add a point: “Moreover…,” “Also…” To give an example: “For instance…” To contrast: “On the other hand…,” “However…” To conclude: “In conclusion…,” “To sum up…”
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: A polite rebuttal
lessons.tip: A rebuttal answers another person’s argument. First show you listened: “I see your point.” Then say where you disagree: “However, …” or “I’m not sure that’s true, because …” Attack the argument, not the person.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Straw man and personal attack
lessons.tip: A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning that makes an argument look stronger than it is. A straw man changes someone’s argument into a weaker one and attacks that. An ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument. Spot them and name them calmly.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: False dilemma and slippery slope
lessons.tip: A false dilemma says there are only two choices when there are more: “Either we ban cars or the city dies.” A slippery slope says one small step will lead to a disaster without proof: “If we allow short breaks, soon nobody will work.” Ask: Are there other choices? Is each step really certain?
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Weigh two arguments
lessons.tip: To decide between two arguments, compare them. Which has stronger evidence? Which reasons connect better to the claim? Are there fallacies? Be fair: state the best version of the other side before you answer it. This is called steelmanning.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)
